stories.title: "Victory For Everyday People": After Six Years, Teton County OKs Affordable Housing
stories.summary: After six years of fighting through red tape, a Wyoming family just got approval to build 387 affordable homes in one of America's wealthiest counties. The landowner's team burst into tears when the vote passed 4-1.
stories.extended_summary: Six years. That's how long the Gill family fought to build the first major non-luxury housing development in Teton County in three decades. When the commission voted 4-1 to approve it, the room erupted — applause first, then tears. "We're all a little dazed," Nikki Gill said. The family is donating land for 70% of the 387 homes to Habitat for Humanity and the Jackson Hole Community Housing Trust, reserved for people making under 120% of the area's median income. They still owe $3.5 million for road upgrades, but after years of negotiation, they finally have a path forward.

stories.extended_summary: In July 2025, Mattoon, Illinois issued a "do not drink" order after toxic algae made the town's main water source dangerous. The culprit: cyanobacteria in Lake Paradise. The solution turned out to be small yellow buoys called Solarafts, topped with solar panels and deployed onto the reservoir. They emit ultrasonic waves that keep cyanobacteria from becoming toxic to humans and animals. The town's water superintendent, Heather McFarland, cast them out this spring like she was sending them to their "summer home." It's a low-cost, solar-powered fix that other rural communities facing similar water crises could replicate.

stories.extended_summary: Paula Clearfield uses a wheelchair for longer distances because walking can be difficult with Parkinson's. But watch her in a training session at the Katz JCC, and you'll see her pushing weighted sleds across the floor. "I have a wonderful trainer, Adam, and he's brought me this far," she says. "If it weren't for him, I wouldn't be where I am physically." Paula is one of the participants in JWell Fit, an eight-week physician-referred program that pairs people with medically informed trainers for twice-weekly workouts. It's designed to bridge the gap between health care and healthy living — and for Paula, it's meant rebuilding strength, mobility, and confidence in what her body can still do.

stories.title: Burned Bobcat rescued from Camp Pendleton fire returns to the wild
stories.summary: A bobcat rescued from the Camp Pendleton fire with severe burns across all four paws has been released back into the wild. After more than two months of intensive care — including light therapy to regenerate his paw pads — the 7.5-pound survivor made a full recovery.
stories.extended_summary: He weighed just 7.5 pounds when he arrived — burned across all four paw pads, emaciated, infested with ticks, and fighting acute kidney injury. The adult male bobcat had survived the Pipeline Fire at Camp Pendleton, and his prognosis was guarded. Over more than two months, the San Diego Humane Society's Project Wildlife team treated him with fluid therapy, pain management, wound debridement, and repeated rounds of Phovia light therapy to stimulate cellular regeneration in his damaged paws. As his wounds closed and his lab work normalized, staff moved him to an indoor-outdoor enclosure, watching on remote cameras while keeping human contact minimal. Then, this week, they opened the gate — and he walked back into the wild.

stories.title: Duck banding in the Centennial Valley helps save the lesser scaup
stories.summary: For 22 straight years, researchers have canoed into Montana's Centennial Valley at dawn to band lesser scaup ducks — building one of the world's longest-running datasets on breeding ducks. The work is helping scientists understand a species that's declined by more than 50% since the 1970s.
stories.extended_summary: At dawn on Lower Red Rock Lake, eleven researchers and volunteers paddle canoes into the fog, guided by the creak of ibis and the chatter of marsh wrens. They're there for the lesser scaup — a duck that was once so common it was taken for granted, until populations crashed by more than 50% since the mid-1970s. This is the 22nd consecutive year of the Lesser Scaup Project, one of the longest-running and most detailed datasets on breeding ducks anywhere in the world. The Red Rock Lakes National Wildlife Refuge, the largest wetland complex in the Greater Yellowstone Ecosystem, hosts thousands of migratory birds. While the refuge was created to protect trumpeter swans, the scaup has become its quiet conservation story — tracked one banded bird at a time.
